desc:
Count the distinct orderings of nums in which every two neighbouring numbers add up to a perfect square (0, 1, 4, 9, 16, ...). Two orderings are different if they differ at some position, so orderings that only swap equal values are counted once.

An array with a single number has no neighbours, so it has exactly one valid ordering.

nums = [1,17,8]  ->  2    ([1,8,17] and [17,8,1])
nums = [2,2,2]   ->  1    (2 + 2 = 4)
nums = [1,2]     ->  0    (3 is not a square)
hints: First work out, for every pair of values, whether their sum is a perfect square. Then the task is to count walks that use every element once.
Build the ordering from the left. The next value must add up to a square with the previous one. To avoid counting equal orderings twice, choose values (with remaining multiplicities), not indices.
Many partial orderings lead to the same situation: what matters is only the remaining multiset of values and the last value placed. Cache the count for that state.
editorial: Count the multiplicity of each distinct value and precompute ok[a][b]: is a + b a perfect square (check with an integer square root). Then run a depth-first search where the state is (how many copies of each value remain, last value placed). From a state, try every distinct value that still has copies left and is compatible with the last value; the recursion ends with 1 when nothing is left.

Choosing values instead of indices makes every distinct ordering appear exactly once, so no deduplication is needed afterwards. The plain search can still be exponential, but memoizing on (remaining counts, last value) bounds the number of states by (product of (c<sub>i</sub> + 1)) · d, at most about 12 · 2<sup>12</sup>, each with at most 12 transitions.
